Dear List,

For your information, the photo-capture of my target species shows a patchy, clustered distribution. Please find attached the raw (i.e., observed) presence-absence map of my data.

The results show a very high value for the decay parameter (phi), while the posterior means and convergence diagnostics (Rhat values) appear to be satisfactory. What confuses me is that both the raw data map as well as a WAIC comparison between the spatial and the analogous non-spatial model (not shown here) suggest the presence of spatial structure in occupancy. But the estimated value of phi seems to suggest that autocorrelation drops to zero at even very small distances.

 

Thanks for any advice

 

 

Warm regards,

 

Singye Wangmo

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: Seeking advice on spatial structure and decay parameter in occupancy modeling
parts:
Hi Singye, 

Hope all is well! Here's a couple of thoughts in regards to your data set: 
  • Given the large amount of clustering in your data set (lots of points very close together, regardless of if the species is detected there or not), you will probably want to increase the number of neighbors in the NNGP to 15. While this likely isn't the main root of the cause here, clustered data can be notoriously difficult to work with in these sorts of spatial models, and using more neighbors (while it will increase the model run time) will ensure that the NNGP approximation is as good as possible. 
  • The spatial component of the model is accounting for residual spatial autocorrelation. So, if the covariates you include in the model do a good job of accounting for the broad spatial correlation that appears prevalent in the raw data map that you attached, then the estimated spatial effects will try to account for any other sort of residual left-over spatial variation. Thus, the phi parameter is only in relation to residual spatial variation that is not accounted for by the covariates in the model. 
  • For situations when working with highly clustered data, sometimes you may want to have a more informative prior on phi in order to prevent the model from "getting stuck" at very small intersite distances. In other words, if there is broad-scale spatial variation that is not explained by the covariates that you want to account for, a more informative prior on phi can be used to try and account for that broad scale variation instead of fine-scale variation. The default prior used in spOccupancy is very vague, and so fine-tuning is often necessary with highly clustered data. I talk about this in detail in this vignette here. 
  • A spatial model can certainly outperform a non-spatial model in terms of WAIC even when the spatial autocorrelation is very fine-scale. That seems to be what you're seeing here. However, if the spatial autocorrelation is very fine-scale, the spatial model likely won't do all that much better at out-of-sample prediction compared to the non-spatial model (or the difference may be smaller compared to in WAIC). So, if one of your main goals is prediction (e.g., making a map across your study area of occupancy probability), I would suggest also using the k-fold cross-validation functionality in the models to assess out-of-sample prediction performance. 
Hope that helps!

Jeff

so we fitted an intercept-only spatial occupancy model to these data with 15 nearest neighbours. Since the range of pairwise inter-trap distances is 0.0001-330 kms, we chose for the spatial range parameter (phi) a uniform prior with c(3/max.dist, 3/min.dist), which yields bounds of about 0 and 21,000 kms. Here are the traceplots for the two spatial parameters:

This shows that the posterior samples for phi are simply draws from the uniform prior, with apparently no contribution from the data. Anybody has an intuition for what is wrong or what we could do better ? I mean, with no covariates to explain the reasonable clustered observed occurrences, we would hope for the spatial parameters to pick up some of this pattern.

Thanks and best regards  --- Marc & Singye

Hi Singye, 

Hope all is well! Here's a couple of thoughts in regards to your data set: 
  • Given the large amount of clustering in your data set (lots of points very close together, regardless of if the species is detected there or not), you will probably want to increase the number of neighbors in the NNGP to 15. Hope that helps!

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: Seeking advice on spatial structure and decay parameter in occupancy modeling
parts:
Hi Marc,

Sorry for my delay in responding. Here's a couple of thoughts on things:
  • Perhaps my use of the word "clustering" was not exactly correct. I mean more that some sites are extremely close while others are very far, so the range of intersite distances is very very big.
  • You could try using more than 15 neighbors, but I don't think that is really what's driving the problem.
  • There is an identifiability problem occurring with sigma.sq and phi. In short, these two parameters are not fully identifiable from each other, and us Bayesian folks rely on the use of priors to be able to estimate the parameters. What appears to be happening here (which is not uncommon, particularly when fitting just an intercept only spatial occ model) is that the model is flip flopping between trying to explain fine-scale spatial autocorrelation (i.e., when phi is large) vs. large-scale spatial autocorrealtion (phi is small). So, you may need to specify an even more informative prior than what you have on phi. If you want to try and explain the large scale spatial patterns, then restrict the upperbound of the prior on phi to something smaller than 1000.
  • There is also an option to specify a uniform prior on sigma.sq (use the name sigma.sq.unif in the priors argument as opposed to sigma.sq.ig). If you restrict the values sigma.sq can take (as opposed to using the default inverse-gamma that is quite uninformative) this could also help improve things. The model is clearly flip-flopping back and forth between trying to accommodate large-scale vs. fine-scale autocorrelation, and often the only choice here is to choose which one you want to try and account for (by specifying a more informative prior).
  • I have a few ramblings on this topic on the package website here.
  • If you're in the mood for a statistical read about this identifiability issue, you can take a look at the paper by Hao Zhang in 2004 here.
Jeff

Hi Marc,

Sorry for my delay in responding. Here's a couple of thoughts on things:
  • Perhaps my use of the word "clustering" was not exactly correct. I mean more that some sites are extremely close while others are very far, so the range of intersite distances is very very big.
  • You could try using more than 15 neighbors, but I don't think that is really what's driving the problem.
  • There is an identifiability problem occurring with sigma.sq and phi. In short, these two parameters are not fully identifiable from each other, and us Bayesian folks rely on the use of priors to be able to estimate the parameters. What appears to be happening here (which is not uncommon, particularly when fitting just an intercept only spatial occ model) is that the model is flip flopping between trying to explain fine-scale spatial autocorrelation (i.e., when phi is large) vs. large-scale spatial autocorrealtion (phi is small). So, you may need to specify an even more informative prior than what you have on phi. If you want to try and explain the large scale spatial patterns, then restrict the upperbound of the prior on phi to something smaller than 1000.
  • There is also an option to specify a uniform prior on sigma.sq (use the name sigma.sq.unif in the priors argument as opposed to sigma.sq.ig). If you restrict the values sigma.sq can take (as opposed to using the default inverse-gamma that is quite uninformative) this could also help improve things. The model is clearly flip-flopping back and forth between trying to accommodate large-scale vs. fine-scale autocorrelation, and often the only choice here is to choose which one you want to try and account for (by specifying a more informative prior).
  • I have a few ramblings on this topic on the package website here.
  • If you're in the mood for a statistical read about this identifiability issue, you can take a look at the paper by Hao Zhang in 2004 here.
Jeff
